A backdoor attack plants a hidden pattern, called a trigger, so that when the trigger is present the model sends the attacked node to an attacker-chosen label. This paper asks what is really happening inside a graph model when that trick works. Instead of only looking for suspicious trigger nodes, it studies the internal channels that become unusually active in a poisoned model. The paper's core claim is that graph structure helps malicious information travel through neighborhoods until particular internal dimensions fire and push the final classification toward the target label.
623.wh: The hard part is that the attack can be designed to look ordinary from the outside. Existing defenses, according to the abstract, mainly try to find and remove triggers by comparing trigger nodes with clean nodes and looking for inconsistencies. That works only when the trigger leaves visible traces: unusual features, strange edges, or a neighborhood pattern that does not fit normal data. The abstract says adversaries can instead build triggers that closely resemble clean nodes. Once that happens, a detector that only asks whether the trigger looks odd is looking in the wrong place. Graphs make this worse because a node is not classified only from its own features. Its neighbors also send information into the decision. A malicious pattern can therefore affect the target indirectly, by shaping the messages arriving from the neighborhood. The defense must explain the path from trigger to wrong label, not merely flag a strange-looking object.
623.naive: A smart beginner would search the graph for suspicious trigger nodes, remove them, and retrain or clean the model. The test would be simple: compare the suspected trigger to normal nodes, and if it has odd features or odd links, cut it out. That fails when the trigger has been crafted to resemble clean nodes. It may pass the same surface checks as harmless data while still causing the model to classify the target node incorrectly. Another beginner move would be to weaken all neighborhood influence, but that throws away the reason graph models work in the first place. Many legitimate labels depend on nearby nodes. The paper therefore looks for a narrower target: the internal channels that carry the backdoor effect.
623.ap: The central move is to shift the defense from the visible trigger to the internal pathway it activates. The paper observes that in backdoored graph models, certain "backdoor neurons" are more likely to fire. Here a neuron means one adjustable internal channel, and an embedding dimension means one coordinate in the compact numeric description the model builds for a node. The trigger does not merely add a bad mark to the input. Through graph propagation, malicious information changes the attacked node's internal description so that these particular channels become active, and that activation steers the final answer toward the target label. Graph Backdoor Neuron Defense, or GBND, then tries to identify, unlearn, and recover those channels. It reverse engineers triggers that activate them, suppresses their harmful effect with asymmetric unlearning, and recovers useful behavior at the neuron level rather than erasing the whole model.
623.mech: The mechanism begins with a graph model that may have been poisoned by a backdoor attack. The inputs are nodes, their features, their neighborhood links, and the trained model's internal activations. First, the defense watches how the model behaves when backdoor behavior is present: which internal dimensions become unusually active, and which of those activations are tied to prediction of the attacker-chosen target label. These dimensions become candidate backdoor neurons. Second, the method uses reverse engineering. In plain terms, it searches backward from the suspicious activation pattern and asks what kind of trigger would reliably make those channels fire. This matters because a visible trigger may look clean, but the internal response it produces can still be distinctive. Third, the defense removes the harmful effect by asymmetric unlearning. The abstract does not give the full algorithmic details, but the phrase implies that the model is not treated uniformly. The defense changes behavior around the harmful channels more strongly than around ordinary useful channels. Finally, recovery restores useful classification capacity at the neuron level, so the model is not simply damaged by deletion. The output is a defended graph model whose suspicious internal route from trigger propagation to target-label activation has been weakened while ordinary graph reasoning is meant to remain usable.
623.math: The first mathematical object is a graph: nodes are the items being classified, and links define which nodes can influence one another. Graph propagation is the rule that lets information move along links. In everyday terms, each node revises its description using its own evidence and evidence arriving from neighbors. That is useful when neighbors are informative, but dangerous when a malicious trigger uses those same roads. The second object is the node's internal numeric description. Each dimension is one channel in which the model stores some learned signal. The paper argues that backdoor attacks concentrate their effect in particular channels, so the defense can score dimensions by how strongly they activate under backdoor conditions and how closely they point toward the target label. The third idea is reverse search: choose an internal effect, then search for an input pattern that causes it. The fourth idea is unlearning, which means changing the model so a learned association no longer controls the answer. The tradeoff is precision versus damage. If the defense changes too little, the backdoor remains. If it changes too much, normal graph classification gets worse. GBND's neuron-level design is a way to make the correction local rather than global.
623.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of graph learning and security. Like other graph papers in the repo, it treats links as channels for evidence movement: neighbors matter because information can travel through the network. Its twist is that evidence movement is not always helpful. An attacker can use the same propagation mechanism that usually improves classification. That connects it to the broader security family, where useful sharing and dangerous leakage are two sides of the same design. It also connects to interpretability, because the defense needs to look inside the model and name which internal channels are carrying the bad behavior. The nearby idea is not merely adversarial robustness as a label; it is controlled trust in a connected system. Graph recommendation, knowledge graph, fraud, and anomaly papers often ask how far signals should travel. This paper asks a sharper defensive version: when a signal travels through the graph, how can we tell whether it is legitimate neighborhood evidence or a planted route to a target label?
623.ww: The approach should work better than trigger detection when the trigger's surface appearance is no longer a reliable clue. If an attacker makes the trigger resemble clean nodes, the outside of the graph can look ordinary. But the attack still has to accomplish something internally: it must move the target node's representation toward the attacker's chosen label. That need creates a possible fingerprint. The model must activate some pathway strongly enough to override normal classification. By focusing on backdoor neurons, the defense looks for the functional consequence of the attack rather than the cosmetic shape of the trigger. Graph propagation strengthens this logic. If malicious information spreads through neighborhoods, then the suspicious effect should appear not only as an input pattern but as repeated activation in particular dimensions. Reverse engineering helps confirm that those dimensions are tied to trigger behavior. Asymmetric unlearning then avoids the blunt cure of weakening the whole graph model. It aims to break the backdoor route while leaving ordinary neighbor-based evidence movement intact.
623.po: The payoff is a defense that treats graph backdoors as a propagation-and-activation problem, not only as a trigger-removal problem. The paper claims to theoretically and empirically show how graph backdoor attacks exploit neighborhood propagation to poison a target node's internal description. It then proposes GBND to identify, unlearn, and recover backdoor neurons. If the claim holds, the defended model can resist triggers that are hard to spot by surface inconsistency checks, because the defense watches the internal channels through which the wrong label is produced. The abstract also reports experiments on four datasets validating GBND, though the provided text is truncated before the full outcome details.
623.limits: The abstract supports the mechanism but does not provide the full proof, algorithm, datasets, baselines, or numerical results. The defense assumes backdoor behavior concentrates in identifiable internal dimensions. If an attack spreads its effect broadly across many channels, or makes harmful channels overlap heavily with channels needed for clean classification, neuron-level unlearning may be harder. The method also depends on reverse engineering triggers that activate suspicious neurons; that search must be accurate enough to avoid mistaking normal class evidence for backdoor evidence. Finally, preserving useful graph reasoning requires that asymmetric unlearning and recovery do not erase legitimate neighborhood signals, especially for classes whose clean patterns resemble the target-label pathway.

624.bp: A sequential recommender is trying to answer a simple but valuable question: after this person has clicked, watched, read, or bought these things in this order, what should be shown next? The hard setting in this paper is the long tail. Most users leave only a short trail, and most items are rarely clicked, so the system has rich evidence for popular items and thin evidence for almost everything else. That matters for any platform with catalogs larger than its visible front page. If rare items never get enough evidence, they stay hidden; if sparse users are treated as unknown, their recommendations collapse toward whatever is already popular. SAGE-Rec serves the practical need to recommend obscure but fitting items without damaging the familiar recommendations that already work for popular items. Before the method name matters, the real object is an uneven history of user-item interactions plus item meanings that may reveal useful relationships not visible in clicks alone.
624.wh: The difficulty is that the evidence is uneven in two directions at once. A popular, or head, item has many interactions, so the system can learn who tends to choose it and after what histories. A tail item has few interactions, so its behavioral record is weak even if its description makes it clearly related to better-known items. Sparse users create the same problem from the other side: their histories are too short to reveal stable taste. A recommender can try to repair this by borrowing semantic information from large language models, meaning text systems that have learned broad relationships among words, descriptions, and concepts. But the abstract says existing uses are shallow: they mostly turn items into isolated numeric descriptions instead of using the larger organization among related items and users. The final tension is the head-tail seesaw. Pushing the model toward tail items can reduce accuracy on head items, while protecting head accuracy can leave the tail invisible.
624.naive: A smart beginner might train a standard sequential recommender on click histories and then add text-derived item descriptions from a large language model. The model would read the user's recent sequence, score candidate items, and choose the highest-scoring next item. For popular items, this can work because there are many repeated cases. For tail items, the method has almost no direct interaction evidence, so their scores are fragile. Another naive repair is to boost tail items by hand, but that can push weakly relevant rare items above genuinely useful popular ones. A third simple idea is to represent each item as one semantic point and compare distances, but that treats semantic meaning as local and isolated. It does not let a rare item inherit structured evidence from several related head items.
624.ap: SAGE-Rec's central move is to make head items and tail items share evidence through global semantic organization rather than through a blunt popularity correction. On the item side, it builds prototypes, meaning representative semantic anchors, and lets a tail item belong to them fuzzily instead of forcing it into one hard group. Fuzzy membership means an item can partly inherit from several related head-item neighborhoods, which fits catalogs where an item may share genre, topic, style, or use case with more than one popular item. On the user side, the method aligns and distills across semantically similar users. Distillation here means using a richer representation as a teacher-like signal for a poorer one, so a sparse user can be enriched by users whose histories point to similar meanings. At the global level, SAGE-Rec adds a light balancing pressure so semantic evidence and collaborative evidence do not overwhelm each other.
624.mech: The input is a set of ordered user-item interactions, item information that can be interpreted by a large language model, and a sequential recommendation backbone model. First, the system uses the language model's semantic organization to describe items by meaning, not only by their raw interaction counts. It then forms item-side prototypes: representative anchors that stand for broader semantic neighborhoods. A tail item is not assigned to a single anchor as if it had only one identity. Instead, the fuzzy-membership mechanism gives it degrees of belonging to related prototypes, especially prototypes connected to head items with stronger interaction records. This lets the tail item receive inherited features from better-observed semantic neighbors. Next, the user side handles sparse histories. Users whose interaction sequences point to similar semantic interests are aligned, and information is distilled between them so a short-history user is represented with more context than their own few clicks provide. The sequential backbone still scores candidate next items from the user's ordered history, so the method does not discard collaborative behavior. Finally, lightweight regularization adds a training constraint that balances semantic and interaction-based signals. The output is a ranked recommendation list intended to preserve head-item accuracy while improving the tail-item positions.
624.math: The main mathematical ideas are sequence prediction, similarity, soft grouping, knowledge transfer, and constrained scoring. Sequence prediction treats a user's ordered actions as evidence about the next action; the order matters because clicking a phone case after viewing phones means something different from viewing phones after buying a case. Similarity turns item or user meaning into a measurable comparison: two items are close if their descriptions and learned semantic context suggest they serve related interests. The danger is that closeness compresses rich meaning into numbers, so the paper's global semantic organization matters because it asks the model to use broader structure rather than one isolated item vector. Fuzzy membership is soft grouping. Instead of saying a tail item belongs entirely to one class, it gives partial weights to several prototypes, which is mathematically useful when categories overlap. Distillation is guided transfer: a richer or more reliable representation shapes a weaker one. Here, better-supported users or item neighborhoods can teach sparse ones. Regularization means adding a penalty for an undesirable training behavior. In this paper, the penalty is light and global: it keeps semantic inheritance and collaborative click evidence in balance, expressing the tradeoff between helping the tail and protecting the head.
624.dots: In the repo's current map, gid 624 is tagged with predicting the next item in a sequence, learning by comparison of similar and different cases, and weighting the parts that are most relevant. That places it at the intersection of recommender systems, language models, similarity, sequence modeling, ranking, and selective weighting. It connects to long-tail recommendation papers such as the repo's SAGERec entry, which also tries to improve rare-item recommendations without sacrificing popular-item utility. It also sits near papers that use language models to repair recommendation signals, including work on popularity bias, multimodal recommendation, graph-LLM alignment, and item-wise training penalties for long-tail LLM recommenders in the recommender-systems family data. The shared pressure is not just recommendation accuracy. It is choosing a small useful set from a huge catalog when past behavior is biased toward what was already exposed. SAGE-Rec's distinct answer is to use global semantic neighborhoods as bridges between well-observed and poorly observed parts of that catalog.
624.ww: The mechanism should help because long-tail failure is partly an information-isolation problem. A rare item may have too few clicks to stand on its own, but it is rarely meaningless. Its text, category, topic, or use case can place it near popular items that have already taught the recommender something about user interest. Fuzzy prototypes make this borrowing less brittle than a hard category label: a niche documentary, for example, might draw evidence from politics, history, and biography-like neighborhoods at the same time. User-side alignment follows the same logic. A sparse user's few actions may be enough to identify a semantic direction, and similar users can provide extra clues without pretending the sparse user has a long history. The balancing penalty matters because borrowed semantic evidence can become too strong. If the model trusts language meaning alone, it may recommend items that sound related but do not fit observed behavior. If it trusts clicks alone, the tail remains starved. SAGE-Rec works by keeping both signals active.
624.po: The claimed payoff is a recommender that improves tail recommendations while preserving head accuracy. The abstract grounds this in extensive experiments across three real-world datasets and multiple backbone models, so the contribution is presented as a plug-in style improvement rather than a result tied to one narrow recommender. In practical terms, the system buys better exposure for semantically fitting rare items and better support for sparse users, while avoiding the common tradeoff where tail gains are purchased by making already reliable popular-item recommendations worse. That is valuable for platforms whose catalogs and users both follow uneven long-tail patterns.
624.limits: The abstract does not prove that semantic similarity always means recommendation relevance. A tail item can sound related to a head item while serving a different audience, price point, quality level, or context. The method also assumes the large language model's semantic organization is useful for the item domain and does not carry harmful popularity or cultural biases into the recommender. User-side distillation assumes semantically similar users can safely share signal; that can fail when two short histories look alike for accidental reasons. The reported evidence covers three datasets and backbone models, but the abstract does not show behavior under new-item launches, adversarial item descriptions, changing user tastes, privacy constraints, or domains where item text is weak.

625.bp: Many real systems are best described as graphs that keep changing. A user follows another user, a transaction appears between two accounts, a road sensor affects a nearby road, or a fact becomes connected to a new fact. The task is not only to read the current graph, but to learn from earlier graph snapshots and make a useful prediction when the next snapshot is similar but not exactly the same. This paper serves that setting. It studies dynamic graph neural networks, which are models that pass information along graph links over time. The problem appears because the world that produced the training graph may not be the same world that produces the test graph. The abstract calls these hidden forces latent environments: background conditions that affect which links appear, how node behavior changes, and which time patterns matter. MoVE is meant to help the model keep the part of graph behavior that travels across environments and reduce the pull of environment-specific accidents.
625.wh: The hard part is that changing graphs mix two kinds of evidence. Some evidence is stable: if repeated interactions between related nodes usually predict a future link, that pattern may remain useful. Some evidence is local to one period or setting: a temporary event, platform policy, synthetic generation rule, or user-behavior regime may make certain messages across edges look important during training but misleading later. A dynamic graph model usually learns by temporal message passing, meaning each node updates its current state using its own past and information arriving from linked neighbors. That is powerful when the same neighbor patterns keep meaning the same thing. It is risky when the pattern is shaped by a hidden environment. The model can mistake an environment clue for a general rule. Then, when the test graph follows a similar but non-identical distribution, the learned rule no longer matches the world. The abstract says these environment-specific factors misguide learning and damage out-of-distribution generalization.
625.naive: A smart beginner would train one dynamic graph model on all available historical data and hope that more history teaches the average rule. The model would pass messages through time, tune itself to reduce prediction error on the training graph, and then reuse the same learned behavior on the test graph. This fails when the training data is a mixture of hidden conditions. Averaging them does not separate a transferable graph pattern from a temporary one. A second naive fix would be to make the model larger, but extra capacity can make the problem worse: the model has more room to memorize environment-specific shortcuts. Another simple fix would be to label each environment and train separate models, but the abstract treats environments as latent, so those labels are not directly observed.
625.ap: The core idea of MoVE is to make hidden environments part of the model instead of pretending they are not there. Since the real environment labels are unavailable, the method creates pseudo-environments: inferred versions of the different background conditions that may have shaped the graph. It uses a hierarchical variational architecture, which means it treats some important internal factors as uncertain hidden causes and estimates them from the observed dynamic graph. Those hidden factors are then extrapolated into a mixture of possible distribution shifts. After that, MoVE uses several experts rather than one shared rule. Each expert can specialize in a different shift pattern, but the training objective also pushes their outputs into agreement where the stable signal should be the same. The result is a model that tries to learn representations that are invariant, meaning useful across shifts, while still acknowledging that different environment pressures exist.
625.mech: The input is a dynamic graph: nodes, links, node or edge information if available, and their ordering over time. A standard dynamic graph model would repeatedly send messages along temporal edges, updating node states as new interactions arrive. MoVE starts from that same kind of temporal message-passing process but asks what hidden conditions could have made those messages look the way they do. First, it builds internal representations of the graph over time, compressing each node's history and neighborhood evidence into learned signals. Second, its variational part treats some of those signals as uncertain hidden variables rather than fixed facts. In plain terms, the model says: this observed graph behavior may have come from several possible background settings, and I should estimate those settings instead of collapsing them into one average. Third, the hierarchy organizes these hidden estimates so they can describe a mixture of distribution shifts, used as pseudo-environments. Fourth, different experts process the representations under these inferred shift views. An expert is a separate decision route with its own learned response to a kind of change. Finally, the training objective compares and aligns expert outputs so that the final representation keeps what agrees across pseudo-environments. The output is a dynamic-graph prediction representation designed to generalize when the test graph is related to, but not identical with, the training graph.
625.math: The main mathematical ideas are graph message passing, hidden-variable probability, mixture modeling, and agreement-based learning. A graph is a map of objects and relationships; message passing is a repeated rule for moving evidence through that map so a node's state reflects both its own history and its neighbors' histories. In a dynamic graph, the map changes over time, so the rule also has to respect order. The hidden-variable idea appears because the abstract says graph generation is strongly influenced by latent environments. A latent variable is an unobserved cause whose effects can be seen indirectly. Here, the model does not observe the environment directly, but it sees the graph patterns the environment helped create. Variational modeling is a practical way to estimate such hidden causes by choosing an approximate belief that makes the observed data plausible. Mixture modeling means the data is not forced into one background condition; it can be explained as several shift types with different weights. The expert mechanism is a controlled division of labor: separate routes handle different inferred shifts. The alignment objective adds a tradeoff. Experts should be flexible enough to represent different environments, but not so separate that they learn unrelated shortcuts. The desired invariant representation is the part of the signal that remains useful across the inferred shifts.
625.dots: This paper sits inside the graph-learning family because it asks how evidence should travel through links when the graph itself is not a clean, fixed object. It connects to the repo's network concept: links are useful roads for evidence, but the method must decide when those roads carry truth and when they carry confusion. It also connects to probability, because MoVE estimates hidden environments and possible shifts rather than assuming the training graph fully reveals the future graph. Its sibling in the same batch, the traffic hypergraph forecasting paper, also treats graph structure and time as inseparable, but it focuses on richer high-order relations for forecasting traffic. The nearby intrusion detection and graph backdoor papers show another pressure in graph learning: messages through neighborhoods can carry harmful or misleading information. MoVE's version of that pressure is not an attacker but a changing environment. Across these papers, the deeper problem is controlled evidence movement under unreliable conditions.
625.ww: MoVE should improve over the naive single-model approach because it refuses to let one training pattern explain every future case. If a temporal message-passing model sees several regimes mixed together, it may learn a rule that works only because one hidden regime dominated the training data. By inferring pseudo-environments, MoVE gives the model a way to separate some of that variation. The mixture of experts then lets different parts of the model become sensitive to different shift patterns, instead of forcing every parameter to serve every condition equally. The alignment step is equally important. Without it, experts could simply specialize in narrow environments and fail when a new graph combines them differently. Aligning their outputs encourages the model to keep features that survive across inferred shifts. The intuitive cause is a separation between accidental and reusable evidence: environment-specific factors can be routed and compared, while stable graph-time structure is encouraged to remain common. That is why the paper's analysis of temporal message passing matters; it identifies where misleading environment information enters the learning process.
625.po: The payoff is better out-of-distribution behavior for dynamic graph neural networks. In practical terms, the model is meant to make predictions on changing graphs when training and test data are similar enough to be related but different enough that ordinary training shortcuts fail. The abstract reports experiments on both real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs and says MoVE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. The capability bought by the method is not just higher score on a fixed dataset; it is a way to model dynamic graphs while accounting for hidden background conditions that shift over time. That matters for web, social, traffic, finance, or knowledge systems where the graph-producing process does not stay still.
625.limits: The abstract does not identify the exact datasets, prediction tasks, or full training objective, so the explanation can only describe the mechanism at the level given. MoVE assumes that useful pseudo-environments can be inferred from the observed dynamic graph and that these inferred shifts correspond to real causes of generalization failure. It also assumes there is some stable signal worth aligning across experts. If the test graph comes from a completely new process, if the hidden environments leave weak traces, or if alignment removes task-specific information that should remain different, the method may struggle. The abstract reports broad experiments but does not prove that the inferred environments are interpretable or that gains hold under every type of graph shift.

626.bp: Modern web services run on hosts that constantly start processes, read and write files, and talk over the network. A serious attack is often not one dramatic event but a chain: one process opens a suspicious file, another process launches from it, and later a network connection carries data out. Provenance-based intrusion detection tries to record that chain as a graph, where the points are system objects such as processes, files, and connections, and the links say that one object caused or influenced another. This paper serves the practical need to notice attacks that were not seen before, using the shape of host activity rather than a fixed list of known signatures. The hard security question is whether such a detector can stay useful when the attacker knows the detector is graph driven and tries to edit the activity graph just enough to hide the attack.
626.wh: The difficulty comes from two facts pulling against each other. Provenance graphs are useful because their structure carries meaning: if a process writes a file and another process later executes it, the direction and order matter. But learned graph detectors can also be brittle. If an adversary subtly changes the graph, the detector may stop seeing the same suspicious pattern even though the underlying attack remains dangerous. A simple defense would train on many altered graphs, but arbitrary graph noise can destroy the very causal story the detector is supposed to learn. Randomly adding or removing links may create impossible histories, such as effects before causes or relationships that could not occur in host activity. Then the model learns tolerance for nonsense, not resilience to realistic disguise. ProvGuard is aimed at this narrow but important tension: make the detector insensitive to harmless, logically valid variations while keeping it sensitive to changes that break the causal meaning of the provenance record.
626.naive: A smart beginner might collect provenance graphs from normal and attacked machines, train a graph detector, and then make it tougher by randomly perturbing those graphs during training. The hope is that if the model has seen many noisy versions, small attacker edits will no longer fool it. This fails because a provenance graph is not just a pile of edges. The edges describe who caused what. Random perturbation can invent activity histories that violate host logic, so the detector may be taught that invalid causal structures are acceptable. Another beginner fix is to hard-code rules about suspicious edges, but previously unseen attacks can follow new paths while still obeying system logic.
626.ap: The core idea is to treat the graph's causal logic as the boundary between useful variation and harmful distortion. ProvGuard does not create training views by changing the graph arbitrarily. It uses logic-aware noise injection, meaning it makes altered versions of a provenance graph only in ways that preserve the semantic rules of host activity. These multiple valid views are then used in contrastive learning, which is a training setup that asks the model to pull together descriptions of the same underlying case and push apart descriptions of different or inconsistent cases. In plain terms, the model is taught: these two graphs may look slightly different, but they tell the same valid activity story; this other change should not be treated as the same story. The central move is therefore not just more data augmentation. It is controlled augmentation guided by the causal meaning of processes, files, and network interactions.
626.mech: The mechanism starts with a host provenance graph. The input records system activity as nodes such as processes, files, and network endpoints, plus directed links that describe causal relations among them. ProvGuard first creates several views of this same graph. A view is an alternate version shown to the learner, but the abstract says these views are produced by logic-aware noise injection rather than arbitrary structural perturbation. That means the alteration must preserve causal semantics: the graph may be varied, but it should still describe a possible host-activity history. Next, the logic-preserving contrastive learning module compares these views. For views that come from the same underlying provenance case and obey the same causal story, the model is trained to produce similar internal descriptions. For views that contain adversarial inconsistencies or represent different behavior, the model is trained to keep their descriptions apart. After this training, a new host graph can be passed through the detector. The detector turns the observed activity graph into a learned description and judges whether it looks like benign host behavior or an anomaly. The output is an intrusion decision or anomaly signal. The abstract also says the system is evaluated on multiple provenance datasets for resistance to graph manipulation attacks, detection accuracy, and efficiency, but the final reported F1-score sentence is truncated in the provided input.
626.math: The first mathematical object is a graph: a set of things and relations among them. Here the things are host objects, and the relations are causal links, so the graph is not merely about closeness; it is about how evidence should travel from one event to another. The second idea is invariance, which means keeping the same judgment when a change should not matter. ProvGuard wants the detector's learned description of a host trace to stay stable under valid graph changes, because a harmless rewrite of the view should not turn normal behavior into an attack or hide an attack. The third idea is contrastive learning, which can be read as comparison training. The learner is given pairs of views and is rewarded for making valid views of the same case close in its internal scoring space while separating views that should not match. The crucial tradeoff is stability versus sensitivity. Too much stability makes the detector ignore attacker edits; too much sensitivity makes it panic over benign variation. Logic-aware augmentation narrows the mathematical comparison task by defining which changes preserve meaning. That makes the comparison less like random noise training and more like learning the equivalence class of causally valid host histories.
626.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of intrusion detection, graph learning, self-supervised comparison, and security. It belongs with fraud and anomaly papers because the target behavior is rare, adaptive, and often absent from a clean labeled catalog. It belongs with graph-mining papers because the evidence is relational: the meaning of a process depends on the files and network actions connected to it. It also connects to the conference's contrastive-learning thread, where models learn from alternate views of the same object instead of relying only on manual labels. The difference is that ProvGuard cannot use arbitrary alternate views, because security provenance has rules about cause and effect. Compared with retrieval or misinformation provenance papers in the repo, this work uses provenance not to audit a document or claim but to detect a hostile activity chain inside a machine. The shared deeper problem is trust in a path of evidence.
626.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it trains the detector on the kind of uncertainty it will actually face. Real host traces can contain benign variation: logging differences, harmless ordering changes, or graph details that do not alter the causal story. An attacker, however, wants a small graph change to make the malicious chain look ordinary. If the model has only learned surface structure, both kinds of change can confuse it. ProvGuard instead teaches the model a sharper distinction. It repeatedly shows valid alternate views of the same provenance graph and asks the model to keep their descriptions together. This builds tolerance for changes that leave causal meaning intact. At the same time, because the training views are constrained by logic, the model is not encouraged to accept causally impossible structures as harmless. The intuitive reason this works is that provenance detection is strongest when it tracks the story of influence, not every incidental edge. A defense guided by that story can ignore harmless graph appearance changes while still noticing edits that disturb the attack's causal footprint.
626.po: The payoff is a host-threat detector designed for previously unseen attacks and for attackers who manipulate provenance graphs to evade detection. The abstract claims that ProvGuard resists graph manipulation attacks better than existing graph-driven detectors while maintaining high detection accuracy and efficiency across multiple provenance datasets. In practical terms, this would make provenance-based intrusion detection more deployable: a security team could rely less on brittle signatures and more on causal activity traces that remain meaningful under valid graph variation. The contribution is especially useful because it addresses both sides of deployment pressure, security resistance and runtime efficiency, rather than treating accuracy alone as the goal.
626.limits: The provided abstract supports the mechanism and evaluation direction but not every operational detail. It does not specify the exact logic rules used by noise injection, the datasets, the attacker capabilities, the completed F1-score value, or how efficiency is measured. The approach assumes that provenance data are captured accurately enough for causal semantics to be meaningful. If logs are missing, forged, or too coarse, valid-looking graph views may still hide important facts. It also assumes that adversarial manipulations create inconsistencies the learned comparison can separate from benign variation. Adaptive attackers who preserve the same logic rules while changing higher-level behavior remain an important open risk not resolved by the abstract.

627.bp: ShadowClone is about identity in a Web3 world where a person may use one identity system across DeFi, GameFi, DAO membership, and other independent domains. The practical need is awkward: a user wants control over private identity data, but services still need to know that the user belongs to some trusted identity domain. At the same time, the system must not let routine movement across domains become a trail that reveals where the user came from or links their activities into a profile. The paper treats decentralized identity as infrastructure, not as a login widget. It asks how many separate communities can recognize a user's right to present credentials while keeping the user's home domain hidden, and how the system can still trace a malicious user when rules are broken. The central object is therefore a proof of legitimacy that should travel across domains without carrying unnecessary identity clues.
627.wh: The hard part is that the system has to satisfy three pressures that pull against each other. First, it must scale as the Web3 ecosystem grows. Existing systems described in the abstract rely on a monolithic committee, meaning one large shared group that handles identity work for everyone. As that committee grows, registration and tracing become bottlenecks. Second, it must protect cross-domain anonymity. A single-domain system can hide a user inside one setting, but frequent movement among DeFi, GameFi, and DAO domains can reveal patterns of affiliation even if the real-world name stays hidden. Third, it must preserve accountability. If a user behaves maliciously, the system cannot simply shrug and say anonymity made tracing impossible. The difficulty is not only hiding information; it is deciding who may learn which hidden fact, at what stage, and with enough public evidence that the tracing process can be trusted.
627.naive: A smart beginner might put all identity records under one global decentralized committee and ask every domain to trust that committee. That gives a simple place to verify credentials and trace abuse, but it recreates the bottleneck the abstract criticizes: every added user and domain increases pressure on the same shared body. Another simple idea is to give each domain its own identity committee and let users present ordinary proofs when visiting other domains. That scales better, but the proof may reveal the user's home domain, so cross-domain behavior becomes linkable. A third naive idea is to maximize privacy by making presentations fully anonymous. That protects users, but it leaves the system with inefficient or impossible tracing when someone uses anonymity to misbehave.
627.ap: ShadowClone's core move is to split identity work by domain while making cross-domain presentations hide the particular domain behind the proof. The sharding architecture partitions the global system into multiple independent domain committees. In ordinary terms, each domain carries its own manageable share of the identity workload instead of forcing one committee to handle the whole ecosystem. To let users move among domains privately, the paper designs a domain-hiding presentation protocol based on an accountable ring signature scheme. A ring signature is a cryptographic signature that says, roughly, one member of this approved set signed, without revealing which member. Accountable means that the hiding is not absolute: a proper tracing procedure can open the result when abuse must be investigated. The paper then makes tracing hierarchical. An opening committee first finds the user's home domain, and the home domain committee traces the specific user within that smaller scope.
627.mech: The input to the system is a multi-domain identity setting: users belong to home domains, domains have committees, and external services need proofs that a user belongs to a trusted set of domains. First, ShadowClone partitions the global identity system into shards, where each shard is an independent domain committee. This changes the workload shape. Registration and local identity management no longer have to pass through one monolithic committee. Next, when a user interacts outside the home domain, the user prepares a domain-hiding presentation. The presentation is built so the verifier can check that the user is backed by one of the trusted domains, but the verifier does not learn which domain is the user's home. The accountable ring signature supplies the cryptographic wrapper for that claim: the visible result proves membership in a set, while the signer remains hidden among possible domain choices. If no abuse occurs, the output is simply a valid cross-domain proof with the home domain concealed. If abuse must be traced, the system follows a two-level opening path. An opening committee first identifies the hidden home domain from the accountable proof. Then that smaller domain committee traces the user's identity within its own records. The abstract states that this tracing process is distributed and publicly verifiable, so outsiders can check that the prescribed procedure was followed.
627.math: The main mathematical ideas are partitioning, set membership proof, anonymity by hiding among alternatives, and controlled opening. Partitioning is the simple idea behind sharding: divide one large workload into smaller pieces so each committee handles a domain-sized problem instead of a global one. The tradeoff is coordination versus speed. More committees reduce local load, but cross-domain recognition must still be consistent. Set membership proof asks a narrow question: can a user convince a verifier that they belong to an approved set without revealing every underlying fact? The ring signature gives one answer. It treats the signer as hidden inside a ring of possible signers or domains; the verifier can check that someone in the ring produced a valid signature, but cannot tell which one. This is privacy math because it deliberately lets one useful signal cross the boundary, legitimacy, while blocking another signal, home-domain affiliation. Accountability adds a second mathematical constraint. The hidden fact must not be visible to ordinary verifiers, yet it must be recoverable through a designated opening process. Hierarchical tracing is a search-space reduction idea: first identify the domain, then search only inside that domain's smaller committee records. Public verifiability means the tracing steps produce evidence that can be checked rather than merely trusted.
627.dots: This paper sits in the privacy, security, decentralization, and efficiency part of the conference map. Like privacy papers, it asks how to let a useful signal leave a private boundary without leaking the underlying person or affiliation. Like security papers, it refuses a privacy story that makes abuse untraceable. Like systems and scalability papers, it changes the architecture because the old bottleneck is part of the problem. The neighboring idea is graph-like partitioning of responsibility: the Web3 ecosystem is not one place but many domains connected by cross-domain interactions. ShadowClone's answer differs from recommendation or retrieval work, but it shares a recurring data-mining pressure: choose the minimum information needed for a decision. Here the decision is whether to trust a user's presentation. The method keeps the trust signal, hides the home-domain signal, and reserves identity recovery for a constrained tracing path.
627.ww: The method should improve on the naive designs because it separates tasks that were previously tangled together. Scaling improves because each independent domain committee handles its own identity work; registration and local tracing do not require a single growing committee to process the entire Web3 population. Cross-domain anonymity improves because a verifier sees proof of membership in a trusted set of domains rather than a direct announcement of the user's home domain. That matters for frequent users: if every DeFi, GameFi, and DAO visit carried the home-domain label, the label itself would become a profiling handle. Accountability remains possible because the ring signature is not merely anonymous; it is accountable. The opening step creates a controlled route from an anonymous presentation back to the home domain, and the second step traces inside that smaller domain. The hierarchy also explains the efficiency claim. Finding the home domain first narrows the later identity search, so tracing does less work than searching globally while still preserving ordinary users' privacy during normal interactions.
627.po: The claimed payoff is a decentralized identity system that handles the multi-domain Web3 setting directly: strong cross-domain anonymity, scalable registration, and efficient accountable tracing. The abstract reports that ShadowClone's registration latency is 10.4% of FADID-TT's and tracing latency is 20% of FADID-TT's, while also offering the stronger privacy guarantee of hiding the home domain during cross-domain presentation. In practical terms, it buys a way for users to prove they come from a trusted domain set without turning every cross-domain action into an affiliation leak, and a way for the system to trace malicious users without falling back to one global committee.
627.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. The trusted domain set must be meaningful; if a verifier trusts weak or compromised domains, a valid membership proof may still be undesirable. The committees, including the opening committee and home-domain committees, must follow the tracing protocol and maintain records that allow tracing within the smaller scope. Public verifiability helps, but the abstract does not detail threat models, committee corruption thresholds, or governance rules for when opening is allowed. The latency comparison is against FADID-TT and is reported through experiments, but the abstract does not show how performance changes under extreme domain counts, uneven domain sizes, repeated cross-domain attacks, or real deployment incentives across independent DeFi, GameFi, and DAO operators.

628.bp: Social event detection is the job of turning a fast, messy stream of public messages into groups that correspond to real happenings: an earthquake, a sports final, a scandal, a protest, or a product launch. The useful output is not a prettier message feed. It is an early map of which posts are talking about the same event, so public agencies, journalists, platforms, and ordinary users can notice what is unfolding. The paper starts from a graph view of this stream. Each message can be treated as a point with words, time, and links to related messages. Many existing systems let nearby messages pass information to one another, then cluster the updated messages. PIGCN asks whether the usual passing rule is too simple. Instead of treating social information like one smooth spreading process, it treats online discussion as something that can surge, fade, return, reinforce, and clash.
628.wh: The hard part is that social messages are short, noisy, and entangled. Two posts about the same event may use different words, appear minutes apart, and come from unrelated users. Two posts using similar words may belong to different events, such as two separate accidents or two rival political stories. A standard graph convolution network tries to solve this by smoothing: each message borrows information from its neighbors, like averaging nearby opinions. That helps when neighbors are genuinely about the same thing, but it quietly assumes that information spreads once and independently. Real discussion does not behave that cleanly. A rumor can be repeated in waves after new evidence appears. A denial can weaken the apparent connection between messages. Competing stories can share vocabulary while pulling attention in different directions. If the model only smooths neighbors, it may blur separate events together or flatten the timing pattern that distinguishes one event from another.
628.naive: A smart beginner would build a similarity graph: connect messages that share words, users, or time windows, then repeatedly replace each message description with an average of its neighbors. After that, cluster the messages whose final descriptions are close. This works for simple cases where one event produces many near-duplicate posts. It fails when the same vocabulary appears across different events, or when an event arrives in several bursts. Averaging treats every neighbor as a soft vote in the same direction. It has no natural way to say that one neighbor should strengthen the current event while another should push it away because it belongs to a competing event.
628.ap: PIGCN's central move is to change what it means for evidence to travel through the message graph. The paper keeps the graph convolution backbone, but replaces the plain smoothing picture with a physics-inspired picture. One part, the Helmholtz Graph Filter, is meant to capture wave-like propagation: signals over the graph can rise and fall, not just diffuse into a bland average. Another part, the Physical Interaction Force mechanism, changes edge strengths as the model learns which messages seem to belong together. Messages judged to be within the same event are pulled closer; messages judged to belong to different events are pushed apart. The system also uses a contextualized text encoder for message meaning and timestamp encoding for when the message appears. The result is a clustering model whose graph operations are designed for multi-wave, interacting social diffusion rather than one-pass smoothing.
628.mech: The input is a collection of social messages for event detection. Each message carries text, a timestamp, and relationships to other messages in a heterogeneous social-message graph. First, the text encoder turns each message's wording into a machine-readable description of what the message is saying; the timestamp encoder adds a description of when it happened, because two similar messages hours apart may mean something different from two similar messages in the same burst. These message descriptions sit on the graph as node features. A conventional graph convolution step would mostly average each node with its neighbors. PIGCN instead sends the graph signal through the Helmholtz Graph Filter, which treats the signal as capable of oscillation across the graph. In plain terms, the model can keep track of waves of support and opposition rather than only smoothing them away. In parallel, the Physical Interaction Force mechanism revises how strong each edge should be. If two messages look like members of the same event, their connection is strengthened, acting like attraction. If they look like different events, their connection is weakened or made separating, acting like repulsion. After repeated propagation and edge adjustment, the model has message descriptions shaped by wording, time, wave-like spread, and learned attraction or repulsion. These final descriptions are then used to cluster messages into detected social events.
628.math: The main mathematical object is a graph: messages are nodes, and edges say which messages may exchange evidence. Graph convolution means updating a node by mixing information from its neighbors. The ordinary version is a smoothing operation, much like replacing a person's view with an average of nearby views. PIGCN argues that this mathematical language is incomplete because online attention does not merely smooth; it can oscillate. The Helmholtz idea comes from wave equations, where a signal can have peaks, troughs, and repeated motion. On a graph, that means decomposing the message signal into patterns over the network and filtering those patterns so that wave-like reinforcement and interference can be represented. The second idea is adaptive edge weighting. An edge is not treated as a fixed fact; it is a quantity the model can adjust according to whether two messages should pull together or push apart. The tradeoff is local evidence versus global separation. Borrowing from neighbors helps recover weak event clues, but too much borrowing merges different stories. Force-like attraction and repulsion give the model a mathematical way to decide when closeness should be increased and when it should be resisted.
628.dots: This paper sits in the event detection theme, but its deeper home is network reasoning. Like traffic forecasting papers that model groups of roads moving together, it treats a graph as a place where signals travel, not just a table of pairwise similarities. Like fraud or security graph papers, it also cares about when edges mislead: a connection can look useful while carrying the wrong evidence. The social-networks family note in the repo describes this paper as addressing the failure of single-pass heat propagation in social event detection. That makes it a sibling of broader graph-learning work that asks how evidence should move through links when the links are noisy, changing, or higher-order. It also touches sequence reasoning because timestamps matter: the same words can mean one thing during the first burst of an event and another thing during a later resurgence.
628.ww: The method should improve over naive smoothing because it gives the model two missing freedoms. First, wave-like filtering lets the graph preserve rise-and-fall structure. If a topic appears, fades, and then returns after a trigger, plain averaging may blur those phases into one weak signal. A wave view can represent repeated bursts and interference between related message patterns. Second, adaptive attraction and repulsion lets the graph correct its own relationships. In a raw message graph, edges are only guesses based on surface clues such as textual similarity, time proximity, or other relations. Some guesses are wrong. By strengthening edges within an event and weakening edges across events, PIGCN can turn the graph from a rough candidate structure into a cleaner event structure. The text encoder supplies semantic clues, the timestamp encoder supplies temporal clues, and the graph modules decide how those clues should travel. The gain comes from matching the model's motion to the claimed motion of social information: multi-wave, interacting, and competitive.
628.po: The payoff is a social event detector that can separate and group messages using more than surface similarity or one-step neighbor averaging. According to the abstract, PIGCN outperforms conventional graph convolution baselines across multiple social event detection datasets and does so while keeping architectural simplicity as a goal. In practical terms, it buys better clustering when events overlap, return in waves, or contain messages that reinforce and interfere with one another. The abstract also says the authors release code, which matters because event detection systems are hard to compare unless the graph construction, timing features, and model details can be inspected.
628.limits: The abstract supports the physics analogy, but it does not by itself prove that social diffusion truly follows the same assumptions as Helmholtz-style wave propagation. The method must rely on graph edges that contain enough useful signal for attraction and repulsion to learn from; if the graph is built from poor links, the model may still move evidence in the wrong directions. It also assumes text and timestamps are informative enough to distinguish same-event messages from merely similar messages. The reported gains are across multiple event detection datasets, but the abstract does not show how the method behaves under major language changes, coordinated manipulation, missing timestamps, or very early detection before enough messages have arrived.

629.bp: A technology-assisted review system is built for a very practical kind of overload: a large collection contains a small set of documents that people truly need to find, and missing those documents is costly. In legal discovery, systematic literature review, and Web-scale information access, the goal is not merely to show a few pleasing results. The goal is high recall: bring as many relevant items as possible into view so experts can make defensible decisions. ALTARS 2026 treats this as a Web problem because the Web is no longer a neat pile of English pages. It contains changing documents, many languages, user-made material, and AI-produced text. The workshop asks how review systems can combine machine help with human judgment while remaining transparent, reliable, and fair. Its object is therefore not one ranking model, but the whole review workflow: retrieval, screening, explanation, governance, and adaptation as the collection changes.
629.wh: The hard part is that review work has two competing demands. The system must shrink a huge pile quickly, but it must not silently discard the rare items that matter. A normal search engine can tolerate some missed pages if the top results satisfy the user. A high-recall review system cannot rely on that bargain, because the missing item may be the legal document, medical study, policy record, or Web evidence that changes the conclusion. Web collections add more trouble. Documents arrive and disappear, languages mix, sources vary in reliability, and AI-produced content can make text look fluent without making it trustworthy. Human reviewers also have limited time, so the system must decide what to ask them to inspect. The abstract emphasizes transparency, fairness, and reliability because automated review can otherwise become a hidden gatekeeper: it decides what humans never see, while giving too little explanation for why those decisions were made.
629.naive: A smart beginner might first index every document, run a keyword search, sort by an automatic relevance score, and ask reviewers to inspect results from the top downward. That is attractive because it matches familiar Web search. It fails when the relevant documents use different words, appear in another language, come from unfamiliar formats, or are mixed with generated content that imitates the topic. It also fails because a high score is not the same as a complete review. If the system cannot explain why items were promoted or skipped, reviewers cannot tell whether the process is fair, whether a group of documents was missed, or whether the machine is repeating biased patterns from earlier review decisions.
629.ap: The central move in ALTARS 2026 is to treat technology-assisted review as augmented intelligence rather than as replacement judgment. The machine should not simply return a final answer; it should help people search, prioritize, explain, and revise the review process. In concrete terms, the workshop points to systems where retrieval models propose likely useful documents, humans provide feedback, explanations show why a document was selected, and governance rules check whether the process is reliable and fair. Large language models can help interpret varied text and generate review support, while knowledge graphs can organize entities and relations so evidence is not just a loose list of passages. The important design shift is workflow-level: the review system must support trustworthy iteration over a changing Web collection, not just produce a ranked page once. The paper is best read as a map of open research problems in that direction.
629.mech: The implied mechanism starts with a collection of Web documents or records that may differ by topic, source, language, format, and time. The review team has an information need, such as finding all legally responsive documents or all studies relevant to a systematic review. A retrieval component first turns that need into candidate documents to inspect. Instead of assuming the first ranking is final, the workflow brings human reviewers into the loop: reviewers judge selected documents, correct mistakes, and give the system evidence about what counts as relevant. The system then updates which documents should be brought forward next. If language models are used, they may help read, summarize, or compare difficult text, but their outputs need to be checked because fluent generated explanations can still be wrong. If knowledge graphs are used, entities, topics, sources, and relationships can be arranged as connected facts, letting the system follow related evidence instead of matching words alone. Explainable components expose the reasons behind selections, such as which text, relation, source cue, or prior reviewer signal mattered. Governance components ask whether the process is auditable, fair across languages or groups, and stable as the Web changes. The output is not only a ranked set of documents; it is a review trail showing what was found, what was judged, what remains uncertain, and why stopping or continuing would be defensible.
629.math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath this agenda. Ranking is the first: each document is given a score so the system can decide which few deserve human attention first. The score is not truth; it is a sorting handle made from text match, source clues, language cues, prior judgments, or graph relations. The danger is that compressing many reasons into one order can hide why a document was buried. Probability is the second idea. In high-recall review, the team wants to know how much of the relevant material has probably been found, even though the unseen pile has not been fully judged. That requires measured uncertainty rather than a confident guess. Learning from human feedback is another idea: the system reuses patterns from reviewer decisions, but must avoid treating early or biased judgments as permanent truth. Graph reasoning adds structured evidence movement. Nodes might be documents, entities, topics, authors, claims, or sources; links say that two pieces of evidence are related. Following links can reveal useful documents that word matching misses, but bad or stale links can spread error. The core tradeoff across these ideas is speed versus completeness, with trust as a constraint: save review effort without hiding uncertainty, unfairness, or unsupported machine reasoning.
629.dots: This paper connects most directly to the conference's broader retrieval and ranking work, because TAR is a severe version of choosing a useful subset from a huge pile. It differs from ordinary search because the cost of a missed relevant item is central, not incidental. It also connects to the neighboring TAR stopping paper in the repo, which focuses on estimating recall early by combining a ranker with a probability sample; ALTARS describes the larger workshop agenda in which that kind of stopping decision belongs. The biomedical screening paper is another sibling: it also uses language models in a human-in-the-loop review setting, but for extracting patient, intervention, and outcome information from full-text studies. Knowledge graph papers are nearby because ALTARS names graph integration as a way to organize review evidence by entities and relations instead of loose text. Responsible AI and data governance are not side topics here; they are part of the retrieval task because transparency and fairness determine whether the review process can be trusted.
629.ww: The agenda works as a research direction because it matches the actual shape of review work. Reviewers do not need a machine that confidently replaces them; they need a machine that spends their attention well and leaves a record they can inspect. Ranking helps because relevant documents are usually not spread randomly. They share words, topics, citations, entities, sources, or relations that can be learned from examples. Human feedback helps because the meaning of relevance is often task-specific: what matters in one legal matter or literature review may not matter in another. Explanations help because they let reviewers catch the system when it is relying on the wrong signal, such as language, source popularity, or generated phrasing instead of substantive relevance. Language models can broaden the system's reading ability across messy Web text, while knowledge graphs can preserve relationships that simple keyword matching misses. The combination should beat the naive approach when each component is used with checks: machine triage for scale, human judgment for meaning, explanation for accountability, and governance for fairness.
629.po: The payoff is a clearer research path for trustworthy Web-scale review. ALTARS 2026 brings together information retrieval, Web science, artificial intelligence, and data governance around systems that can search large heterogeneous collections while keeping people in control. The capabilities it points toward are practical: finding more relevant material under limited review time, adapting to dynamic and multilingual Web content, using language models and knowledge graphs without giving up auditability, and making automated review decisions more transparent and fair. Because this is a workshop abstract, the concrete result is not a measured accuracy gain; it is a venue and agenda for shaping the next generation of TAR systems.
629.limits: The abstract does not prove that any specific TAR system is reliable, fair, multilingual, or Web-scale in deployment. It names important components, including human-in-the-loop learning, explainable AI, language models, knowledge graphs, and governance, but does not specify an implemented pipeline, dataset, evaluation protocol, or failure analysis. The agenda assumes reviewers can provide useful feedback, explanations can be made understandable, and graph or language-model support can be checked rather than blindly trusted. It also assumes fairness can be operationalized across sources, languages, and groups. Those are hard conditions. Without careful measurement, augmented review can still miss rare evidence, inherit biased judgments, overtrust generated text, or create transparency that looks persuasive without being truly diagnostic.
